opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so a lot of it comes from watching how people talk past each other when they compare data systems. Someone will say "System A is ten times faster than System B," and that might be completely true for the benchmark they ran, but it tells you almost nothing about whether it'll be better for *your* workload. There are just so many dimensions that matter: how big the data is, how often it changes, whether you're doing lots of small point lookups or big scans, how many concurrent users you have, what latency you need versus throughput, how much you care about freshness, cost, governance, and so on.

In research we see this all the time. A paper optimizes one axis really well, and it's a real contribution, but then practitioners try to apply it and discover that their bottleneck was somewhere else entirely. Maybe the query engine was fast but most of their time went into data loading, or into dealing with messy schemas, or into the cost of keeping a cluster up 24/7 for a workload that only runs an hour a day.

So having a taxonomy is really about giving people a shared vocabulary. If we can say, "This workload is high-concurrency, low-latency, small data, frequently updated," versus "This one is batch, huge data, latency-tolerant, cost-sensitive," then it becomes much clearer which design choices and which benchmarks actually apply. It also helps us as system builders see where the gaps are, the combinations of requirements that no existing system handles well, which is often where the most interesting new work comes from.

And it matters even more now with AI workloads in the mix. You've got things like retrieval, feature serving, and agents issuing tons of queries automatically, and they stress systems in pretty different ways than a human analyst running dashboards. Without a structured way to describe those differences, it's very easy to build or pick the wrong tool.

r001.rationale: The response says workloads differ across many relevant dimensions and that a taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for describing those differences, helping people compare workloads and choose applicable designs and benchmarks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the reason I care about this is that when people talk about data systems, they tend to collapse everything into one number. It's either "how fast is it" or "how much does it cost," and then you get these benchmark wars where one vendor runs a query a little faster than another and that becomes the whole conversation. But that's almost never how workloads actually behave in production.

What we see at Databricks, and honestly what I saw back in the Spark days too, is that a real workload has several independent axes. There's the data layout and format, there's the query pattern, whether it's mostly scans or point lookups or joins, there's concurrency, how many users or jobs are hitting the system at once, there's the freshness requirement, is this a batch report that runs nightly or something that needs to reflect events from a few seconds ago. And then there's the operational side: how much tuning does it take, how does it behave when the data skews or the schema changes, what happens when something fails halfway through.

The problem is that if you don't name those dimensions explicitly, you end up optimizing for the one that's easiest to measure. And then you get a system that wins TPC-DS and falls over the moment a hundred analysts start running ad hoc queries against it. So a taxonomy is really a forcing function. It makes you ask, for this particular workload, which of these actually matters, and which of these am I willing to trade off. A lot of the time the answer is that you don't need the fastest engine, you need the one that's predictable along the two or three axes your business actually cares about.

The other thing it does is it gives you a vocabulary for comparing systems that were designed for very different points in that space. A streaming system and a warehouse and a lakehouse are not really competitors in a single race; they're making different bets. And once you have the dimensions laid out, you can have a much more honest conversation about where each one is strong and where it's not, instead of pretending there's a single winner.

r001.rationale: The response says a taxonomy makes the workload dimensions explicit and prompts people to consider which ones matter, covering more than a single speed or cost metric.

astra-6.text: Well, data workloads are very diverse, so it’s hard to say that one system is simply faster or better than another. Are you doing short queries that need low latency, or large batch jobs where throughput matters? How much data are you processing, and how often does it change? How many users are accessing it concurrently? Those dimensions lead to different design choices. A taxonomy helps you understand what a benchmark is actually measuring and whether the result applies to your workload. It also helps explain why you might need different systems for different parts of an application.

r001.rationale: The response says a taxonomy helps interpret benchmarks and judge whether results apply, but does not clearly say it helps cover all relevant evaluation dimensions.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, data workloads are very diverse, so it’s hard to say that one system is better than another without understanding what you’re asking it to do. Are you running short queries that need a response in milliseconds, or long analytical jobs? How much data are you processing? How frequently does it change? How many users are accessing it at once?

The point of a taxonomy is to make those requirements explicit. Then you can understand which architectural choices make sense, where a system’s strengths are, and whether a benchmark actually represents your workload. Otherwise, you can end up comparing systems that are optimized for very different problems.

r001.rationale: The response says a taxonomy makes requirements explicit and gives examples of workload dimensions, but it does not clearly state that it helps ensure all relevant dimensions are covered.
